exercises.title: Explaining why a 50-page PDF blew the API budget
exercises.situation: A teammate is confused why sending a long internal PDF into the LLM API call is so much more expensive and slower than a short one, and asks you to explain what's actually going on before they file it as a bug.
exercises.beginnerResponse: It's expensive because the document is long, so obviously it costs more to process. We should probably just not send such big documents.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It never explains the actual billing and performance mechanism — tokens, not words or pages — so the teammate walks away with no way to estimate cost themselves or recognize the pattern next time. It also jumps to a blanket 'don't send big documents' rule instead of naming the real options: trimming, chunking, or compressing context, each with different tradeoffs. There's no mention of the context window limit that would make this fail outright past a certain size, not just get expensive.
exercises.professionalResponse: The cost and latency scale with tokens, not pages or words — the API breaks text into tokens, which are often sub-word pieces, and both the request and the response are billed per token, so a 50-page PDF can easily be tens of thousands of tokens before the model generates a single word back. That also interacts directly with the model's context window: every model has a maximum number of tokens it can hold across the system prompt, the conversation history, and this document combined, and if we're close to that ceiling, the call doesn't just get expensive, it can fail outright or silently truncate older content. Rather than banning long documents, I'd manage the context window as a budget: decide what actually needs to be in the prompt versus what can be dropped, retrieved only when relevant, or summarized down. If we're sending this document repeatedly, context compression — summarizing or extracting just the relevant sections instead of the full text — would cut both the cost and the latency on every call after the first one. And if this pattern happens often with the same provider, it's worth checking whether their API supports prompt caching for the repeated portion of the context, since some providers charge and process a cached prefix much more cheaply than a cold one. I'd also flag that tokenizer behavior isn't perfectly predictable from word count alone — code, non-English text, and unusual formatting can tokenize less efficiently than plain prose, so the actual token count is worth checking directly rather than estimating from page count.

exercises.title: "Can't we just train it on our documents?"
exercises.situation: A stakeholder asks, "Can't we just train the AI on our internal documents so it knows them?" and wants you to explain how you'd actually approach that.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Sure, we can train it on our documents so it knows them and can answer questions about them.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It agrees to 'train' the model without checking whether the stakeholder actually means fine-tuning or something else, and it never distinguishes that from retrieval-augmented generation — which is almost always the right fit for 'answer questions about our documents.' It has no mention of embeddings, chunking, or a vector database, so there's no real plan behind the agreement, and it sets an expectation (a model literally trained on the docs) that is slower, pricier, and harder to keep current than what's actually needed.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd clarify terms first, because 'train it on our documents' usually means one of two very different things. Fine-tuning actually adjusts the model's internal weights using examples, which is expensive, needs a real training dataset of input/output pairs, and has to be redone every time the documents change — it's a poor fit for 'know our documents and answer questions about them.' What we almost certainly want instead is retrieval-augmented generation, RAG: we don't change the model at all, we chunk the documents into manageable pieces, convert each chunk into an embedding — a numeric representation of its meaning — and store those in a vector database. When a question comes in, we retrieve the most relevant chunks by comparing embeddings and hand them to the model as context, so it answers using content pulled live from the actual current documents instead of anything baked into its weights. That means when a document changes, we just re-embed and re-index it — no retraining, no waiting days for a fine-tuning job, and the model is answering from whatever the documents say today, not whatever they said when it was last trained. Fine-tuning would only become the right conversation if we needed the model to adopt a specific tone, format, or specialized skill consistently, which is a different problem than 'knows our documents.'

exercises.title: What "few-shot" and "chain-of-thought" actually mean
exercises.situation: A junior teammate's prompts are inconsistent, and they ask what terms like "few-shot" and "chain-of-thought" mean and whether they actually matter or are just buzzwords.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Those are just fancy words for writing good prompts. You basically just ask it clearly and it should work.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It dismisses real, distinct techniques as interchangeable buzzwords instead of explaining what each one specifically does, so the teammate learns nothing they can actually apply. 'Ask it clearly' gives no concrete technique to try when a prompt is failing, and it misses that these techniques solve different problems — ambiguity, multi-step reasoning, consistency — so picking the wrong one, or none, is exactly why their prompts are inconsistent.
exercises.professionalResponse: They're not interchangeable, and each one solves a different problem. Zero-shot means you ask directly with no examples, relying entirely on the instructions; few-shot means you include a small number of example input/output pairs in the prompt so the model can infer the pattern you want, which is usually the fastest fix for 'it keeps giving the wrong format.' Chain-of-thought is different — it's asking the model to reason step by step before giving a final answer, which measurably helps on problems that require multi-step logic, and tends to do nothing for a problem that's actually just a formatting or clarity issue. A system prompt is where you set the model's role, constraints, and voice once so it doesn't drift across turns, and a prompt template is how you standardize a prompt's structure so it's reusable and testable across many inputs instead of hand-written each time. For inconsistent output on the same kind of question, I'd start by checking whether the issue is ambiguity — few-shot usually fixes that — or reasoning failures on harder cases, where chain-of-thought helps. If I needed a single answer to be more reliable rather than just better-reasoned, I'd also consider self-consistency: sampling the model multiple times and taking the most common answer, which trades extra cost for reliability on harder questions. The deeper reason any of this works at all is in-context learning — the model adapting its behavior within a single prompt based on patterns shown to it, without any retraining — which is worth knowing conceptually even though it's not something you tune directly.

exercises.title: Not every tool call is "the AI doing something"
exercises.situation: A product manager used "ReAct," "tool calling," and "orchestrator" interchangeably in a planning doc for a new agent feature. Explain what each term actually means and why the distinction matters for what gets built.
exercises.beginnerResponse: They basically all mean the same thing — the AI uses tools to do stuff and figures out the steps itself.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It collapses three distinct, well-defined concepts into one vague idea, so the PM has no way to tell from the planning doc whether they're describing a single agent calling tools, a specific reasoning pattern, or a multi-agent system with very different build complexity. There's no mention of the agent loop that ties these together, and nothing about why picking the wrong architecture term in a planning doc leads to wrong scope and timeline estimates.
exercises.professionalResponse: They're related but distinct, and mixing them up in a planning doc leads to the wrong scope estimate. Tool calling, also called function calling, is the mechanism: the model is given a schema describing available functions and decides when to invoke one, with what arguments, instead of just generating text. The agent loop is the broader cycle that wraps that: plan what to do, act by calling a tool, observe the result, and repeat until the task is done or it decides to stop. ReAct is a specific, well-known pattern for structuring that loop, where the model explicitly interleaves reasoning steps with actions, which tends to make the model's decisions more inspectable and often more reliable than just letting it call tools freely. Orchestrator/worker is a different axis entirely — it's about whether this is one agent with many tools, or a coordinating orchestrator agent that delegates subtasks to specialized worker agents, each with its own narrower tool set. A multi-agent system is the general term for any architecture using more than one agent, which can include orchestrator/worker but isn't limited to it. For this planning doc, I'd pin down two separate questions: which reasoning pattern governs each agent's loop, and whether this is a single agent or a multi-agent system — because the second question alone changes the build timeline significantly, and conflating the two makes the estimate unreliable. I'd also flag that reliability degrades in ways worth planning for explicitly: agent behavior is inherently non-deterministic, so the same input won't always produce the same tool call, and what the team sometimes calls 'context rot' — degraded decision quality as an agent's running history fills up with its own prior steps — is a real failure mode worth designing memory and state around, not an edge case to handle later.

exercises.title: REST status codes aren't just "error" or "not error"
exercises.situation: A new hire's integration code only checks for HTTP status 200 and retries blindly on anything else. A recent outage got worse because of this. Explain what's wrong and the vocabulary they're missing.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Status 200 means it worked and anything else means it broke, so you should just retry until you get a 200.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It collapses a whole category of distinct, meaningful status codes into a binary 'worked or broke,' which is exactly the bug that made the outage worse — blindly retrying on a client error that will never succeed, or retrying a non-idempotent request that already partially succeeded, both cause real harm. There's no mention of which errors are worth retrying, how to retry safely, or any pattern for handling the ones that aren't just 'try again.'
exercises.professionalResponse: Status codes are categories, not a binary. 4xx codes mean the client did something the server won't accept — a bad request, missing auth, a rate limit — and retrying the identical request will just fail again; some of those, like a 429 rate limit, specifically tell you to slow down, not retry immediately. 5xx codes mean something failed on the server's side and might be transient, so those are actually worth retrying, but with exponential backoff — waiting longer between each retry — rather than hammering an already-struggling service immediately. The deeper issue in this outage is idempotency: if the request wasn't idempotent, meaning running it twice has a different effect than running it once, then blindly retrying after a timeout can duplicate the side effect even if the first attempt actually succeeded and only the response got lost. I'd also check whether this integration handles pagination and webhooks correctly, since treating a paginated response as complete or missing a webhook retry can produce silent data gaps that look fine until someone notices missing records days later. The fix here isn't 'retry on failure,' it's a response-code-aware strategy: don't retry 4xx at all except where the code tells you to with a different action, retry 5xx with backoff, and make sure the operation being retried is actually safe to repeat — or add an idempotency key if it isn't. Longer-term, a circuit breaker — temporarily stopping calls to a service that's failing repeatedly, rather than continuing to retry into it — would have limited how much this outage could cascade.

exercises.title: A RAG assistant that gives confident wrong answers
exercises.situation: An internal RAG knowledge assistant that used to answer accurately has started giving confident, wrong answers to questions it previously handled fine. Explain how you'd investigate.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd check if the documents are still there, and if everything looks fine I'd probably just re-index everything to be safe.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It jumps straight to a blind, expensive fix — re-indexing everything — without first separating whether this is a retrieval problem (wrong or no relevant chunks found) or a generation problem (right chunks, but the model ignores or misreads them). It never actually looks at what was retrieved for a failing question, which is the single most informative piece of evidence available, and it has no way to know afterward whether the re-index actually fixed anything.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd start by separating this into two possible failure categories, because they need completely different fixes: either retrieval is returning the wrong chunks, or retrieval is fine and the model is misusing or ignoring good context. I'd pick a handful of the now-failing questions and look directly at what the retrieval step actually returned for each — the real chunks, not an assumption about them. If the retrieved chunks are irrelevant or missing the answer entirely, that points to a retrieval problem: maybe the embedding model was changed or upgraded without re-embedding the existing index, which would silently desync the vectors from the model now generating query embeddings; maybe chunk boundaries are splitting answers across chunks awkwardly; or maybe this needs re-ranking or hybrid search that isn't in place. If the retrieved chunks do contain the right answer and the model is still getting it wrong, that's a generation-side faithfulness problem — the answer isn't grounded in what was actually retrieved, which citation and source attribution would have caught immediately, since a properly-cited wrong answer would show it's citing something that doesn't support the claim. I'd also check whether this is isolated to certain question types or broadly affects everything, since a broad regression right after a deployment points to something systemic like a model or embedding change, while an isolated pattern points to specific document or chunking issues. Once I've isolated which side it is, I'd fix that side specifically — re-embed with the correct model, adjust chunking, add re-ranking, or tighten the prompt's instructions to answer only from retrieved context — and validate against a held-out set of questions with known-correct answers, comparing pass rate before and after, rather than spot-checking the one or two complaints that got reported.

exercises.title: An agent that won't stop calling the same tool
exercises.situation: An agent got stuck overnight repeatedly calling the same search tool without making progress, running up a large API bill. Explain how you'd investigate and prevent it from happening again.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just add a limit so it can't call the tool that many times, and that should stop it from happening again.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It proposes a cap without ever diagnosing why the agent got stuck in the first place, so the same underlying confusion could easily resurface as a different repeated tool call, or the agent could just fail silently right at the new limit instead of actually completing the task. There's no mention of logs, reasoning traces, or distinguishing a true infinite loop from an agent oscillating between two near-equivalent actions, both of which need different fixes.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd start by pulling the actual audit log of the agent's reasoning and tool calls overnight, since 'stuck calling the same tool' can mean a few different things that need different fixes. If it's genuinely calling the identical tool with identical arguments over and over, that's usually a sign the agent isn't registering that the tool already returned a result, or the result isn't being fed back into its context correctly, which is a bug in how the agent loop observes its own tool outputs. If instead it's alternating between two or three very similar calls without converging, that's closer to oscillation — the agent repeatedly deciding a slightly different version of the same action is worth trying, which usually points to the task being underspecified or the stopping condition being unclear to the model. I'd check whether reflection or self-correction logic exists at all, since an agent with no way to recognize 'this approach isn't working' will keep trying it indefinitely. Once I know which pattern this is, I'd fix that specific cause — correct how results get fed back into context, clarify the task's success condition, or add explicit reflection steps — rather than only adding a hard cap. That said, I'd still add cost and action limits as a safety net regardless of root cause, because even a well-diagnosed agent should have a hard ceiling on tool calls and spend per task as a last line of defense, not the only line of defense. To validate, I'd re-run a similar task in a sandboxed environment and confirm the agent either completes it or stops cleanly well under any limit, and I'd check that the audit log clearly shows why it stopped, so a future repeat of this is diagnosable in minutes instead of discovered the next morning as a bill.

exercises.title: The assistant got noticeably worse after a model update
exercises.situation: Shortly after the underlying model provider pushed a version update, users report the assistant's answers have gotten noticeably worse. Explain how you'd investigate.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd probably just switch back to the old model version if we can, since it sounds like the new one is just worse.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It treats 'users say it's worse' as sufficient evidence to act on, with no attempt to measure the regression objectively, and it assumes rolling back is possible or free, when some providers deprecate old versions on a schedule that may not leave that option open for long. It never considers that the real issue might be the prompt itself being tuned to the old model's quirks rather than the new model being categorically worse at everything.
exercises.professionalResponse: Before touching the model version, I'd quantify the regression rather than relying on anecdotal reports, by running our existing eval dataset — or building one if we don't have it — against both the old and new model versions and comparing pass rates directly. If a formal benchmark exists for this kind of task, I'd also check that, since it gives a reference point independent of our own possibly-biased eval set. I'd specifically check whether this is a broad quality drop or isolated to certain question types, because a narrow pattern often points to prompt sensitivity to the model change — our system prompt and few-shot examples may have been implicitly tuned to the old model's specific quirks, and a new model can interpret the same instructions differently even when it's generally more capable. I'd also check the provider's changelog for what actually changed in this version, since providers don't always swap the model behind a stable version string transparently, and it's worth confirming we're not dealing with an unannounced silent model swap rather than the version bump we think we approved. Once I can see the actual pattern — broad regression versus isolated prompt sensitivity versus a provider-side change we didn't fully account for — I'd act specifically: adjust the prompt for the new model's behavior, or roll back if the regression is genuine, broad, and reproducible against our eval set, with the understanding that providers often deprecate old versions on a timeline, so rollback might only buy time, not be the permanent fix. Either way, I'd put this exact eval dataset into regular use as a regression test run on any future version change, including rollbacks, rather than waiting for user complaints to be the detection mechanism again.

exercises.title: New container instances time out right after a scale-up
exercises.situation: During a traffic spike, autoscaling added new container instances for the AI app, but the first several requests to each new instance are timing out. Explain how you'd investigate.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd probably just add more instances ahead of time so this doesn't happen, since it sounds like we just need more capacity.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It assumes the problem is a lack of capacity rather than a startup-time problem with each new instance, which are different issues with different fixes — more instances that each still take too long to become ready doesn't actually solve anything. It never considers model weight loading time, which is often the real, AI-specific driver of slow cold starts, and it has no plan to confirm that new instances were even the ones timing out versus some other cause.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd first confirm this is actually a cold start problem and not something else coincidentally correlated with the scale-up — I'd check whether the timing out requests specifically landed on the newly created instances, and whether the timeouts cluster right after instance creation and then stop. Assuming that's confirmed, cold start for a typical web service is usually about process startup, but for an AI workload specifically, the dominant cost is often model weight loading time: pulling potentially multi-gigabyte model weights into memory, or onto a GPU, before the instance can serve a single request, which can easily take far longer than a normal container's startup. I'd check whether the container image includes the model weights baked in versus pulling them at startup, since the latter adds network transfer time on top of load time, and whether a multi-stage build is being used to keep the runtime image lean without sacrificing that. I'd also check whether there's a health check or readiness probe in place — if the load balancer starts routing traffic to a new instance before it's actually finished loading its model, that's exactly this symptom, and the fix might be entirely in how readiness is signaled rather than in the loading time itself. Depending on what I find, the fix is one or more of: baking weights into the image to skip the pull step, using a GPU-enabled container configuration that avoids redundant transfer, adding a proper readiness probe so traffic isn't routed too early, or pre-warming a buffer of instances before a predictable spike using cost-aware scaling rather than reacting purely to load after the fact. I'd validate by triggering a similar scale-up in a test environment and measuring the actual time from instance creation to first successful response, confirming it's now under whatever SLA we need, rather than assuming any single change fixed it.

exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It treats prompt editing as trial and error with no systematic way to check whether a new tweak fixes all four cases without silently breaking a fifth, which is exactly the problem that caused this in the first place. exercises.professionalResponse: First, I'd pull up exactly what changed in the system prompt and run it against all four scenarios — the one it was meant to fix and the three it broke — to confirm the actual before-and-after behavior rather than going on secondhand reports. exercises.title: Should this be RAG or a fine-tuned model?
exercises.situation: The team needs an assistant that answers questions about internal policy documents that change every few weeks. Explain how you'd decide between RAG and fine-tuning, and why.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd go with fine-tuning since that makes the model actually learn the policies instead of just looking things up each time.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It picks the architecture based on a vague notion of 'actually learning' rather than the concrete requirement that matters most here — documents changing every few weeks — and it never names the real cost of fine-tuning on that cadence: retraining repeatedly, or living with increasingly stale answers between retrains. It treats 'looking things up' as inherently worse than 'learning,' when for this specific requirement it's the opposite.
exercises.professionalResponse: The deciding factor here is the update cadence, and that points clearly toward RAG, not fine-tuning. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into the model's weights at a point in time, so with policies changing every few weeks, we'd either be retraining on a tight, costly cycle, or accepting that answers reflect outdated policy for however long we wait between retrains — and policy questions are exactly the kind of thing where a confidently wrong, outdated answer is a real liability. RAG keeps the documents external to the model: we chunk and embed the current policy documents into a vector database, and retrieve the relevant chunks at query time, so updating the knowledge is just re-embedding the changed documents, typically minutes of work, not a retraining cycle. The underlying reason is the difference between parametric and non-parametric knowledge — fine-tuning stores knowledge inside the model's parameters, which is frozen between training runs, while RAG keeps it external and fetched fresh each time, which matches a frequently-changing source much better. There are cases when RAG is the wrong answer — if the task needed a specific consistent tone, format, or specialized skill applied across every interaction rather than factual lookup, fine-tuning or even a well-designed system prompt might fit better — but 'answer accurately from documents that change often' is squarely RAG's use case, not fine-tuning's. I'd validate the choice isn't just theoretical by actually testing retrieval quality against a sample of real policy questions, including some from recently-changed documents, to confirm the freshness advantage holds in practice and not just in theory.

exercises.title: One agent with many tools, or three specialized agents?
exercises.situation: A new feature needs an agent that can search internal docs, query a database, and send notifications. Explain how you'd decide between one agent with all three tools versus an orchestrator delegating to three specialized worker agents.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just give one agent all three tools since that's simpler to build and we don't need to overcomplicate it with multiple agents.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It optimizes purely for initial build simplicity without weighing the real tradeoff against it — a single agent with many tools has to choose correctly among a growing, potentially overlapping tool set on every turn, which gets harder and less reliable as more tools are added, and it never considers whether these three capabilities actually need to be coordinated versus just available. There's no consideration of what happens as this feature grows, or what state and memory needs each capability actually has.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd decide based on how independent these three capabilities actually are and how much coordination overhead a split would add, not just on what's simplest to build today. A single agent with all three tools keeps things simple short-term, but tool selection and routing gets harder as the tool set grows or as tools start to look similar to the model, increasing the chance it calls the wrong one or in the wrong order. An orchestrator/worker pattern — a coordinating agent that delegates to specialized workers for search, database queries, and notifications — tends to make each worker's job narrower and more reliable, since a worker focused on one domain has less to choose between, but that comes at the cost of coordination overhead: more latency from agent-to-agent handoffs, more surface area for something to go wrong between them, and more complexity to build and debug. For this specific case, I'd look at whether these three capabilities are used together in a single task often, which argues for one agent that can freely sequence them without handoff overhead, or whether they're more separable — e.g., sending a notification is a final, independent step that doesn't need deep context from the search and query steps — which argues for separation of concerns via an orchestrator/worker split. I'd also factor in state and memory needs: if the database query results need to inform what search is done next, that's context that's easier to manage within a single agent's loop than passed between separate workers. My inclination for exactly this combination is a single agent with well-scoped tools and good tool descriptions as context, since three well-defined tools isn't yet the scale where orchestrator/worker earns its coordination cost — but I'd revisit that the moment a fourth or fifth capability gets added, or if any one of these three starts needing its own complex sub-reasoning.

exercises.situation: A new feature needs an LLM in production. Explain the tradeoffs between using Azure OpenAI Service and self-hosting an open-source model, and how you'd decide.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Azure OpenAI is probably easier so let's just use that, self-hosting sounds like a lot of extra work for no real benefit.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It dismisses self-hosting without naming any of the real reasons a team might actually choose it — data residency requirements, long-term cost at high volume, or needing a model Azure OpenAI doesn't offer — and it treats 'easier' as the only decision criterion, ignoring compute options, cost management, and compliance considerations that could make the 'easy' choice the wrong one for this specific feature.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd decide this based on a few concrete factors rather than defaulting to whichever sounds easier. Azure OpenAI Service gives us a managed endpoint with built-in scaling, monitoring, and content safety APIs, backed by managed identities and Key Vault for credentials, which meaningfully reduces operational burden — we're not managing GPU infrastructure or model updates ourselves. Self-hosting an open model means choosing our own compute options for AI workloads, provisioning and managing that infrastructure, and taking on responsibility for scaling and monitoring that a managed service would otherwise handle. The factors that would actually push toward self-hosting are data residency — if this data legally or contractually can't leave a specific environment we control, a managed cloud endpoint might not satisfy that regardless of how convenient it is — and cost at high, sustained volume, where a well-utilized self-hosted deployment can beat per-token managed pricing once volume is high enough to justify the fixed infrastructure cost; that crossover point is a real calculation, not a guess. I'd also check whether the feature needs a capability or model family that Azure OpenAI doesn't offer, which would make self-hosting close to mandatory rather than a choice. If none of those apply — no hard data residency constraint, moderate and uncertain volume, a model Azure OpenAI already offers — the lower operational burden of the managed service wins by default, and total cost of ownership favors it too once we count the engineering time self-hosting would actually require, not just the infrastructure bill. I'd validate this decision isn't premature by revisiting it once we have real usage data: actual volume, actual cost per request, and confirmation of whether any compliance requirement we didn't fully scope up front turns out to matter.

exercises.title: Why the vector index needs its own scaling plan
exercises.situation: As the app scales, a teammate assumes the vector database will just scale automatically along with the application servers. Explain why that assumption is wrong and what actually needs to be planned.
exercises.beginnerResponse: It should scale fine, we can just add more servers if it gets slow, same as everything else.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It treats the vector database as an interchangeable stateless service like an application server, when it's actually built around specific indexing algorithms with their own, different scaling characteristics and tradeoffs. It never names what indexing strategy is in use, what the recall-vs-latency tradeoff actually is, or that adding more compute doesn't automatically fix a poorly-chosen index structure the way it might fix a stateless app server under load.
exercises.professionalResponse: A vector database doesn't scale the same way a stateless application server does, because its performance depends on the indexing strategy underneath it, not just raw compute. Most vector databases use an approximate nearest neighbor search rather than an exact comparison against every vector, because exact search doesn't scale past a relatively small number of vectors — HNSW and IVF are the two common approaches, and each has different tradeoffs in build time, memory use, and query speed as the number of vectors grows. The key tradeoff to plan around is recall versus latency: a more thorough search finds the truly closest matches more reliably but takes longer, and most indexing strategies expose parameters to tune that tradeoff deliberately rather than getting it by accident. Just 'adding more servers' can help with throughput — serving more concurrent queries — but it doesn't fix a fundamentally mismatched index configuration if, say, recall is too low because the index was tuned for speed when it needed to prioritize accuracy, or if hybrid search combining vector and keyword matching is needed but isn't in place. Metadata filtering is another scaling consideration — filtering by metadata at query time has its own performance cost that compounds as the dataset grows, and some vector databases handle that more efficiently than others. For a real scaling plan, I'd look specifically at scaling a vector database as its own topic: sharding or partitioning the index as vector count grows, choosing an indexing strategy and its parameters deliberately based on our actual recall and latency requirements, and load-testing query performance at realistic scale rather than assuming it degrades gracefully like a typical web service would. I'd validate this by benchmarking query latency and recall at our current scale and at a projected future scale, so we have real numbers instead of an assumption that more servers solves it.

exercises.title: Blue-green or rolling update for the model endpoint?
exercises.situation: The team is about to roll out a new model version behind a production endpoint. Explain which deployment strategy you'd use and why.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd just update the endpoint to the new model directly, since it should work fine and we can fix it after if something's wrong.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It has no rollout strategy at all — a direct cutover with no staged exposure means any regression hits 100% of traffic immediately, with no fast way back, and 'fix it after' isn't a plan when the thing being swapped is a model whose quality can only really be judged against real traffic, not a code diff that's obviously right or wrong. It never names a rollback strategy, so there's no clear path back if the new version turns out to be worse.
exercises.professionalResponse: For a model version change specifically, I'd avoid a direct full cutover, because model quality regressions aren't always obvious from testing alone and are best caught against a small slice of real traffic first. Blue-green deployment would stand up the new model version fully in parallel and switch traffic over all at once, which gives a clean, fast rollback by switching back to the known-good version, but it still means 100% of traffic hits the new model the moment the switch happens. Rolling updates gradually replace instances running the old version with the new one, which is good for ordinary software updates but for a model change specifically, I'd actually prefer something closer to a canary release: routing a small percentage of real traffic to the new model version while most traffic stays on the proven one, and watching quality metrics on that slice before increasing the percentage. Even before that, for a model swap I'd consider shadow traffic — running the new model against a copy of real requests without actually serving its responses to users — purely to compare its outputs against the current model's on real traffic, which catches regressions with zero user-facing risk before any real cutover begins. Whichever staged approach I use, I need a clear rollback strategy defined ahead of time: how fast can we revert, and what's the trigger — a specific drop in whatever eval or quality metric we're watching, not just a vague 'if something seems off.' I'd validate the new version is actually ready for full rollout by comparing its real-traffic quality metrics against the old version's baseline on the canary or shadow slice, and only proceed to full traffic once that comparison is clearly favorable, not just 'nothing obviously broke.'

exercises.professionalResponse: I wouldn't promise it won't happen again, because that's not something any LLM-based system can honestly guarantee, and promising it sets up a worse conversation the next time it happens. exercises.title: Justifying a pricier model to a cost-conscious PM
exercises.situation: A product manager wants to switch a customer-facing feature to a cheaper, faster model to cut costs. Explain the tradeoffs in business terms.
exercises.beginnerResponse: The cheaper model might not be as good, so we could lose some quality, but it would save money.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It states the tradeoff so generically that it gives the PM nothing to actually decide with — no sense of how much quality might be lost, on which kinds of requests, or what that quality loss would cost the business in return for the savings. It treats this as a vague gut call rather than something that can actually be tested and measured against this specific task before committing either way.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd frame this as a specific tradeoff to measure, not a vague feeling to decide on. Cost, latency, and quality move together but not proportionally — a cheaper, faster model isn't a straight discount on the same quality, it's a genuinely different capability level, and how much that matters depends entirely on what this feature actually needs the model to do. I'd start by running our current eval set, or building one from real examples of this feature's typical requests, against both models, so we have an actual quality comparison on tasks that matter here instead of a general reputation for being 'worse.' If the gap is small or nonexistent on our specific use case, switching is close to a free win — lower cost and lower latency with no real quality cost to the customer. If the gap is meaningful, I'd translate it into business terms: what's the error budget here, meaning how much quality degradation can this feature actually tolerate before it measurably hurts customer trust, support ticket volume, or conversion, versus what the cost savings are actually worth at our current volume. A model switch that saves a modest amount per request but increases support escalations or damages a customer-facing experience can cost more than it saves, just in a less visible place on the budget. I'd also point out that 'quality' isn't one undifferentiated score — the right task-fit evaluation might show the cheaper model is actually fine for simple requests and weak specifically on edge cases, which could support a hybrid approach: route easy requests to the cheaper model and only use the pricier one where it actually earns its cost. I'd bring back real numbers from testing against our own use case before recommending either way, rather than a general sense that 'cheaper is probably fine' or 'cheaper is probably risky.'

exercises.title: Explaining why the agent can't just issue the refund itself
exercises.situation: A stakeholder is frustrated that the new support agent asks for human approval before issuing refunds, and wants it to "just handle it." Explain the reasoning.
exercises.beginnerResponse: It's safer to have a human check it, so we added that step just in case something goes wrong.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: "Just in case" doesn't explain what specifically could go wrong or why refunds in particular deserve a checkpoint when other actions might not, so the stakeholder has no way to evaluate whether the tradeoff is actually worth the friction it adds. It never distinguishes refunds from lower-stakes actions by any concrete property, so it sounds like blanket caution rather than a deliberate, justified design decision.
exercises.professionalResponse: The reasoning isn't blanket caution, it's specific to what makes a refund different from most other actions this agent might take: it's both financially consequential and hard to reverse cleanly once it's processed, especially at any real volume. I'd frame it around blast radius and reversibility — the key questions for deciding what an agent should be allowed to do autonomously aren't 'is the agent smart enough' but 'how much damage could a single mistaken action cause, and how easily can we undo it.' A wrong answer in a chat is low blast radius and fully reversible: we just say something different next time. An incorrectly issued refund is real money that's genuinely left the business and that we may not get back by simply flipping a switch, so it sits in a different risk category entirely regardless of how reliable the agent generally is. The approval checkpoint design matters here too — it's not meant to approve every refund manually forever, it's specifically there for the cases where the agent's confidence or the request's specifics cross some threshold worth a second look, and I'd design escalation so routine, low-risk refund requests can eventually be fully automated once we have the data to trust that specific pattern. I'd also point out that even with approval checkpoints in place, we still need defined undo and rollback strategies for whatever mistakes do get through human review, since human approval reduces risk but doesn't eliminate it. If the friction here is the real complaint, the fix isn't removing the checkpoint, it's tightening what triggers it — tuning where that confidence threshold sits based on real outcome data — so routine cases get approved near-instantly while only the genuinely risky edge cases actually wait on a human.

exercises.title: Explaining a prompt injection incident to leadership
exercises.situation: An attacker got the support bot to reveal part of its system prompt and internal instructions via a crafted message. Leadership wants a plain-language explanation of what happened and what's being done about it.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Someone tricked the bot into leaking some internal info, but we patched it so it shouldn't happen again.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It doesn't name what actually happened in a way leadership can reason about risk from, doesn't explain why a single patch isn't the same as the problem being fully solved, and promises a result — 'it shouldn't happen again' — that overstates what any single fix against this class of attack can honestly guarantee.
exercises.professionalResponse: What happened is called prompt injection: an attacker crafted a message specifically designed to get the model to ignore its actual instructions and instead follow instructions embedded in their input, which in this case caused a specific, named failure called system prompt leakage — part of our internal instructions ended up in the response. I'd be direct with leadership that this is a known, actively studied risk category for any system built on an LLM, not a one-off bug unique to our implementation, and that no single fix makes a system permanently immune to every variation of this kind of attack — that's exactly why the right response is defense in depth, meaning several independent, overlapping protections, rather than one patch we consider the final word. What we're doing specifically: we've closed the exact pattern that was exploited, we're adding tighter output handling so even if an attacker crafts a new variant, sensitive internal instructions are checked for and withheld before a response goes out, and we're expanding our red-teaming effort to proactively look for similar gaps ourselves instead of waiting for them to be found in production. I'd frame the business risk honestly: the actual damage here was limited to information leakage about our own prompt design, not customer data or an unauthorized action, and I'd be specific about that boundary rather than letting it sound more serious than it was, or less. Going forward, I'd commit to tracking this as an ongoing category we monitor and red-team against on a recurring basis, with incident response steps defined ahead of time, rather than treating today's fix as the end of the conversation.

exercises.title: Making the case for NOT fine-tuning, in dollars
exercises.situation: A stakeholder read that fine-tuning "makes the AI better" and wants it for a feature that doesn't actually need it. Explain the real cost/benefit in business terms.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Fine-tuning is expensive and takes time, so we probably shouldn't do it for this feature.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It asserts the conclusion without naming any of the actual costs involved, and 'probably shouldn't' isn't a business case a stakeholder convinced by something they read elsewhere is likely to accept — it needs concrete numbers and tradeoffs, not a hunch stated with low confidence.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd make the case in concrete terms rather than just asserting it's not worth it. The real cost of fine-tuning isn't just the compute for one training run — it includes building and curating a labeled training dataset, the engineering time to set up and evaluate the fine-tuning process, and critically, the ongoing maintenance burden: every time the base model updates or our requirements shift, we either re-validate the fine-tuned model against the new baseline or run the whole process again, which a prompt change doesn't require at all. There's also a real opportunity cost: the engineering time spent on a fine-tuning project is time not spent on other features, and for this specific case, I don't think fine-tuning would even move the quality needle, since the actual limitation here isn't a specialized skill or consistent tone the model is missing — standard prompting or retrieval covers that. I'd point to the when-to-fine-tune-vs-prompt decision framework directly: fine-tuning earns its cost when a task needs a very specific, consistent output style or skill across every single interaction that prompting genuinely can't achieve, not for general quality improvement, which is what I think is actually being hoped for here. I'd also flag a real technical risk worth stating in business terms: fine-tuning carries a chance of catastrophic forgetting, where the model gets worse at other things it currently does well while gaining the narrow skill we fine-tuned it for — that's a regression risk on top of the direct cost, not a pure upside. My recommendation is to try a prompt-based improvement first, since it's close to free to test and iterate on, and only revisit fine-tuning if we hit a specific, well-defined limitation that prompting genuinely can't solve — at which point I'd bring back real cost numbers for that specific case, not a general one.

exercises.title: Proving the RAG assistant actually got better
exercises.situation: After tuning chunk size and adding re-ranking, explain how you'd prove to the team that RAG quality actually improved, not just assume it did.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I tried a few questions and the answers looked better, so I think it's an improvement.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: A handful of spot-checked questions isn't a measurement, it's an impression, and 'looked better' doesn't distinguish whether retrieval got better, generation got better, or just these particular questions happened to go well this time. There's no comparison against a consistent before-and-after baseline, no separation of retrieval quality from answer quality, and no real metric the team can trust or reproduce.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd prove this with a held-out eval set of representative questions with known-correct answers, run against both the old and new configuration, rather than a handful of spot checks. I'd measure retrieval and generation separately, because chunk size and re-ranking changes affect retrieval directly, and I want to know if that's actually what improved rather than assuming a better final answer means retrieval got better. On the retrieval side, I'd look at something like retrieval precision and recall — whether the chunks returned actually contain the answer, and whether we're missing chunks that do — since chunk size changes can improve one while hurting the other depending on how it shifted document boundaries. On the generation side, I'd check faithfulness versus relevance separately: an answer can sound relevant to the question while not actually being supported by what was retrieved, or be perfectly faithful to an irrelevant chunk, and these are different failure modes with different fixes. Citation and source attribution helps here concretely, since checking that citations genuinely support the claims in each test answer is a direct, auditable faithfulness check, not just a vibe. I'd report the actual before-and-after numbers on all of these dimensions, not just a percentage of 'looks good' answers, and I'd specifically check whether the improvement held across different question types, not just the ones that motivated the chunk size change in the first place, since a fix targeted at one failure pattern can sometimes trade away performance on another. Only once I have real pass-rate deltas across retrieval precision/recall and faithfulness/relevance would I call this a proven improvement, and I'd keep this eval set as a standing regression check for any future retrieval tuning.

exercises.title: Validating a fine-tuned model before shipping it
exercises.situation: A newly fine-tuned model is ready to potentially replace the production model. Explain how you'd validate it before making that switch.
exercises.beginnerResponse: If it does well on the training examples, it should be good to ship.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: Checking performance on the training examples themselves is close to meaningless — a model can memorize them and still fail on anything slightly different, which is exactly the overfitting risk that makes this validation step necessary in the first place. There's no held-out test set, no comparison against the current production model's baseline, and no consideration of whether the model lost general capability while gaining whatever it was fine-tuned for.
exercises.professionalResponse: Performance on the training examples themselves tells us almost nothing useful — a model can score perfectly there through overfitting, essentially memorizing the training data, while performing poorly on anything it hasn't seen before, which is precisely the risk this validation step needs to catch. I'd evaluate it on a held-out set that was never part of the fine-tuning data, built the same way we'd build any eval dataset: representative of real production traffic, with known-correct expected outputs. I'd compare its performance directly against the current production model's baseline on that same held-out set, using the same benchmarking approach we'd use for any model comparison, so we have an apples-to-apples pass-rate delta instead of an isolated score. Critically, I'd also test it on tasks outside the specific fine-tuning focus, because catastrophic forgetting is a real risk — the model could have gained whatever narrow skill we fine-tuned it for while quietly getting worse at other things it used to handle fine, and the training-examples check would never catch that since it only looks at the narrow target skill. I'd run this as a proper regression test against our full existing eval suite, not just the fine-tuning task's own test set, specifically to catch any such regression elsewhere. If the fine-tuned model passes the held-out set for its target skill, matches or beats the baseline on the rest of the eval suite, and shows no regression on tasks outside its fine-tuning focus, that's what I'd call ready to ship — and I'd keep monitoring its real production performance closely after the switch, since a held-out eval set, however good, is still a proxy for real traffic, not a guarantee.

exercises.title: Red-teaming your own support bot before launch
exercises.situation: Explain the validation process you'd run on a new AI feature before launch, beyond just manually trying a few questions yourself.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd try asking it a bunch of different questions myself and make sure the answers look reasonable before we launch.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: Manually trying questions has no defined coverage — there's no way to know what proportion of realistic scenarios, including adversarial ones, actually got exercised, so passing a self-directed spot check provides very little real assurance. It never considers that someone might deliberately try to misuse the system, and it has no repeatable process that could be run again after the next change.
exercises.professionalResponse: I'd build this around three distinct activities, because 'try a bunch of questions' doesn't have defined coverage and misses adversarial behavior entirely. First, building eval datasets properly: a representative set of realistic questions with known-correct expected answers, covering the actual range of what users will ask, not just the cases that come to mind easily. Second, automated eval metrics run against that set, covering accuracy, relevance, and faithfulness specifically, so we get a repeatable, objective pass rate instead of a subjective 'looks reasonable' judgment. Third, and this is what a self-directed spot check entirely misses, red-teaming our own AI app: deliberately trying to get it to misbehave — leak information it shouldn't, say something harmful, or be manipulated via prompt injection — because a well-intentioned tester asking normal questions will never find what an adversarial user looking for a way to break it will find. I'd also include human evaluation processes for the subset of outputs that automated metrics can't reliably judge on their own, like nuanced tone or genuinely ambiguous correctness calls. The thing I'd be honest with the team about is coverage: however much realistic and adversarial testing we do, it's worth being explicit about what proportion of the real scenario space it actually represents, rather than assuming a passing test run means the system is safe against anything a real user, or attacker, might eventually try. This whole process should become a standing regression suite we re-run before every future change, not a one-time pre-launch checklist, since the next prompt or model update could reintroduce exactly the issues this caught.

exercises.title: Proving the autoscaled AI app can handle the surge
exercises.situation: Ahead of a planned marketing launch expected to spike traffic, explain how you'd validate the AI app's autoscaling and reliability beforehand, rather than just trusting it'll work.
exercises.beginnerResponse: Autoscaling should handle it automatically, so I think we'll be fine once the traffic comes in.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: It treats autoscaling as a guarantee rather than a configuration that needs to be tested under realistic conditions, and it has no plan to actually simulate the expected load ahead of time, which means any problem — slow cold starts, cost blowing past budget, or a queue backing up — would only be discovered live, during the actual launch, when it's most costly to fix.
exercises.professionalResponse: I wouldn't trust autoscaling to handle this without testing it against something close to the real expected load first. I'd run a load test that simulates the anticipated traffic pattern — not just average load, but the actual spike shape, since a sudden surge stresses autoscaling very differently than a gradual ramp. During that test, I'd specifically watch for cold starts on newly spun-up instances, since model weight loading time can make early requests to new instances slow or fail exactly when we need them most. I'd check whether queueing and async processing is handling any burst beyond immediate capacity gracefully, with reasonable wait times, rather than requests simply timing out or failing outright. I'd also look at tail latency specifically, not just the average: a p50 latency that looks fine can hide a p99 that's badly degraded, and the actual user experience during a spike is disproportionately shaped by that worst case, not the average case. Caching strategies for repeated or similar requests would help absorb some of the load without hitting the model at all, so I'd confirm those are actually in place and effective for this traffic pattern specifically. And since a marketing launch means a predictable spike, I'd use cost-aware scaling deliberately — pre-warming a buffer of instances ahead of the expected surge rather than relying purely on reactive autoscaling, which has to detect the load increase and then wait for new instances to become ready, exactly when those instances are least ready to help. I'd validate all of this with real load-test numbers against defined thresholds — target p99 latency, acceptable error rate, and a cost ceiling — before the launch, not by assuming the system will behave the way it does under ordinary, lower, more gradual traffic.

exercises.title: Showing a prompt change didn't just fix the obvious case
exercises.situation: Explain how you'd validate a prompt change thoroughly before merging it, beyond just confirming it fixed the one reported complaint.
exercises.beginnerResponse: I'd run the one example that was failing a couple of times and if it works now, I'd merge the change.
exercises.whyBeginnerIsWeak: Running one example a couple of times says nothing about whether the fix generalizes to other cases, and it ignores that LLM outputs are probabilistic — passing once or twice isn't strong evidence the fix is reliable even for that exact case, let alone the rest of the eval set this prompt needs to keep working for.
exercises.professionalResponse: Fixing the one reported case is necessary but nowhere near sufficient. First, I'd run this exact case multiple times, not once or twice, since LLM outputs are probabilistic and a couple of passing runs isn't strong evidence the fix is reliably working even for this one case — that's where self-consistency-style multiple sampling actually earns its keep in validation, not just in production answers. Second, and this is the step a narrow fix skips, I'd run the full existing prompt eval set, since a change narrow enough to fix one case can still regress others it wasn't tested against — that's exactly the kind of regression testing prompts is meant to catch before a merge, not after. Third, I'd think about statistical significance and sample size honestly: if the eval set is small, or if I'm only checking a handful of cases per category, a passing run might just be noise rather than a real improvement, so I'd want enough representative cases per category to trust the result, not just a comforting pass/fail count. Fourth, for a change significant enough to matter, I'd propose A/B testing it against a slice of real production traffic before a full merge, comparing real-world outcomes rather than only our offline eval set, since our eval set is itself a proxy for real usage and might not perfectly represent it. I'd only consider this ready to merge once the original case passes reliably across repeated runs, the full eval set shows no regression, and either the sample size is large enough to trust the result or a live A/B comparison backs it up — not based on a single pass on the one case that prompted the change in the first place.

vocabulary.definition: Running a prompt's eval set automatically as part of the development process, rather than manually and inconsistently.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's what makes running the full eval set on every change practical and consistent, rather than an occasional manual effort.
vocabulary.example: This should run through automated prompt testing on every change, not just when someone remembers to check manually.

vocabulary.definition: Constructing a representative set of test cases to validate prompt behavior across realistic scenarios.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: Its size and representativeness directly determines whether a passing result can actually be trusted.
vocabulary.example: If the eval set is too small, a passing result might just be noise rather than a real fix.

vocabulary.definition: Running the same prompt multiple times and checking consistency of the result, trading extra cost for a more reliable read on actual behavior.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: It's directly applicable to validation itself, not just production answers — running the fixed case multiple times checks whether the fix is actually reliable, not a one-off lucky pass.
vocabulary.example: Running the original case multiple times, the same idea behind self-consistency, is how I'd check the fix is actually reliable, not a lucky pass.

vocabulary.definition: General statistical concepts about whether a result reflects a real effect or could plausibly be noise, and how many samples are needed to tell the difference.
vocabulary.whyItMatters: They're directly relevant here because LLM outputs are probabilistic — a handful of passing examples isn't automatically strong evidence of a real, reliable improvement.
vocabulary.example: With a small sample size, I wouldn't trust a passing result as statistically significant evidence the fix actually works.

languageUpgrades.weak: I'd run the failing example a couple times and merge it if it works.
languageUpgrades.professional: I'd run the original case multiple times for reliability, then the full eval set for regressions, before considering this ready to merge.
languageUpgrades.whyStronger: Replaces a minimal, single-case check with a reliability check plus a full regression check.

languageUpgrades.weak: It passed, so the fix works.
languageUpgrades.professional: A couple of passing runs isn't strong evidence on its own, since outputs are probabilistic — I'd want enough samples to trust the result statistically.
languageUpgrades.whyStronger: Names the specific reason a pass alone isn't sufficient evidence.

languageUpgrades.weak: We'll just ship it to everyone since it looks fixed.
languageUpgrades.professional: For a change this significant, I'd A/B test it against a slice of real traffic first, rather than rolling it out to everyone based on an offline check alone.
languageUpgrades.whyStronger: Proposes a staged validation against real usage instead of an immediate full rollout.

sayItLikeASenior.beginnerStatement: It worked when I tried it, that's good enough.
sayItLikeASenior.suggestedProfessionalVersion: I'd want it to pass reliably across several repeated runs, not just once, since LLM outputs are probabilistic.

sayItLikeASenior.beginnerStatement: We only need to check the case that was reported.
sayItLikeASenior.suggestedProfessionalVersion: I'd run the full eval set too, since a fix narrow enough to solve one case can regress others it wasn't tested against.

sayItLikeASenior.beginnerStatement: Our eval set passing means it'll work in production.
sayItLikeASenior.suggestedProfessionalVersion: Our eval set is a proxy for real usage, so for a significant change I'd still want to confirm with an A/B test against real traffic before trusting that fully.

selfAssessmentRubric: Did you propose running the original case multiple times rather than once or twice?
Did you propose running the full existing eval set to check for regressions elsewhere?
Did you raise sample size or statistical significance as a reason not to over-trust a small passing result?
Did you propose A/B testing against real traffic for a significant change?
Did you use at least 4 of the vocabulary terms above naturally?
exercises.verbalRehearsalPrompt: Present your validation plan out loud as if explaining to a teammate why their one-case check isn't enough to merge. Then repeat it from memory, keeping the reliability-then-regression-then-evidence structure and at least four vocabulary terms.
